title: A handful of leaves
hookLine: the Buddha holds a few leaves: what I have taught is this; what I know is the forest; I taught what helps (SN 56.31)
last: THREE TURNS — NO CLAIM UNTIL ALL TWELVE ARE CLEAR.

cards: A cook copies out a family recipe on the back of an envelope: five ingredients, three steps. She knows far more: the history of the dish, why the onions go in first, the aunt who taught her.
She leaves it out on purpose, because the friend holding the envelope needs to make dinner tonight. The handful of leaves came up briefly on the last day of year one.
Today it's back in its home, the book of the Connected Discourses on the four truths, read slowly: the setting, the full list of reasons, and the test it leaves behind.

teach.b: The Buddha is staying in a grove of simsapa trees near Kosambi. He picks up a few leaves and asks the monks: which are more, these in my hand or the leaves in the grove overhead? The leaves in the grove, they say, by far.
In the same way, he says, the things I have directly known but not taught are far more. Then the part that's easy to skip. Why hasn't he taught them?
Because they aren't beneficial. They don't belong to the basics of the holy life. They don't lead to letting go, to calm, to peace, to direct knowing, to awakening, to nibbana.
And what has he taught? This is dukkha. This is its arising.
This is its ending. This is the way. Because that does help.
It leads to letting go, to calm, to peace, to awakening. So the handful isn't a random sample. It's a careful choice, and the filter is simple: does it help?
The Buddha isn't hiding anything mysterious behind his back, or saying the rest of the forest is forbidden.
He's a teacher who knows what a student needs, the way the cook knows her friend needs dinner.
Fittingly, this sutta sits in the book of the four truths, the Buddha explaining why the last two weeks have been about four sentences and not four hundred.
And it hands us a test for anything we read, watch, or worry about: does this lead to calm and freedom, or just to more noise?

how: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of the simsapa leaves to explain why the teaching centers on the four noble truths and on what leads to peace, rather than on every question that can be asked.

o: a leaf the monks used to wrap alms food
a kind of tree, like the grove he stood in
a sacred tree no one may ever cut down

games.q: match the pieces of the simsapa sutta.
p: what he knew but didn't teach
does it lead to peace and awakening?

s: the Buddha said the leaves in the forest were secret teachings
he left them out because they don't help toward letting go, peace and awakening.
the handful the Buddha taught is the four noble truths
dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way.
the story takes place in a simsapa grove near Kosambi
that's the setting the sutta gives.

games.q: you're a monk in the simsapa grove. the Buddha says he knows far more than he's taught. why, he asks, hasn't he taught it?
o: because you aren't ready for secrets.
because it doesn't help toward peace and awakening.
games.why: he says the rest isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to letting go, calm, peace and nibbana; the four truths do.

practice: Hold a few leaves loosely in your open palm, or anything small, a few coins or dried beans, and feel how little they weigh. Then, breathing slowly, let your mind fill with everything you're carrying today: plans, news, worries.
For each one, ask quietly: is this in the handful, or is it the forest?

wordCard.voice: Simsapa. The grove of trees where the Buddha held up a handful of leaves, teaching only what helps toward calm and freedom.

orig.note: Pali siṃsapā: the simsapa tree (often identified as Indian rosewood), whose grove gives the sutta its name.

carryVoice: Your line: only what helps. Four sentences, chosen with care, out of a whole forest. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: SN 56.31 (Simsapa Sutta, the handful of leaves)
